items.summary: This paper offers a candidate descriptive model based on the author’s retrospective account of internal agent-like experience during a past period of social isolation, emotional distress and perceived high cognitive load. It is a non-clinical reconstruction, not a technique, treatment or recommendation. No contemporaneous physiological, behavioral or neuroimaging measurements were recorded. The Opposition–Load–Coupling vocabulary organizes reported phases of self-talk, opposition, felt load, perceived coupling, autonomy, boundary degradation and disengagement. These are reported experiences and interpretive constructs, not demonstrated causal mechanisms. Claimed benefits and harms are unmeasured first-person reports. The Shared Value Anchor is an untested candidate predictor, not an established stabilizer or necessary condition. The case does not establish whether value conflict preceded initial boundary degradation or distinguish the proposal from a simpler load-based account. The model is situated alongside dialogical-self, Internal Family Systems, predictive-processing, imaginary-companion, writer-agency and tulpa literature. Any incremental contribution lies in the proposed coupling vocabulary and separately testable value-anchor hypothesis, not in discovering internal multiplicity or proving a new mechanism. Safety: do not intentionally induce or replicate the conditions described. This is the author’s own past experience, published at the author’s direction; no formal ethics approval or exemption is claimed. Version 4 incorporates author-adopted revisions following advisory and changed-text checks, including prior-involved AI reviewers. Those checks are not independent peer review, clinical validation or evidence of effectiveness.

items.summary: Lecture 1 formulated the recommendation problem in abstract terms: a set of users U , a set of items I , and a preference function r(u,i) that must be estimated for the pairs that have not been observed. Every algorithm studied in this course, however, operates on concrete data rather than on abstractions. The quality of a recommender system is therefore bounded by the quality, the structure, and the representation of the data from which it learns. In practice, improving the data frequently brings larger gains than changing the algorithm. A sophisticated model trained on noisy, biased, or poorly prepared data produces poor recommendations, a principle often summarized as garbage in, garbage out . This lecture therefore addresses three questions: è Which data does a recommender system collect, and what do these data really mean? è How can these data be organized and represented so that algorithms can process them? è How must the data be prepared and partitioned before a model is built and assessed? After studying this lecture, the reader should be able to: · Identify the sources and categories of data used in a recommender system; · Characterize explicit and implicit feedback, including their strengths and weaknesses; · Construct a user–item matrix and interpret its sparsity; · Represent users and items as vectors built from interactions and descriptive features; · Apply the main preprocessing operations to ratings and implicit signals; · Split a dataset correctly and avoid information leakage. The path followed by the data throughout this lecture is: Data sources → Feedback signals → User–item matrix → Vector representations → Preprocessing → Data splitting
items.title: Lecture Notes on Recommender Systems

items.summary: We present DECAF, a privacy preserving neural speech codec that obfuscates a speaker's voice while preserving linguistic content while maintaining automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance at very low bitrates, inspired by decaffeination. At the transmitter end, speech is encoded into speaker independent content embeddings, which are compressed using residual vector quantization and transmitted without any speaker related information. At the receiver, a canonical speaker embedding, shared a priori between endpoints, is used for waveform reconstruction, enabling deterministic and consistent obfuscation of a speaker's voice. The proposed framework leverages an information bottleneck applied to self supervised representations, along with a separate speaker embedding branch, to achieve effective speaker content disentanglement. We further incorporate a CTC-based auxiliary objective, encouraging content representations that are well aligned with downstream ASR tasks. We show that DECAF operating at a bit rate of 0.5 kbps achieves an Equal Error Rate (EER) of up to 43.5% for a speaker verification system, while maintaining competitive ASR performance, yielding a relative reduction in word error rate of 33.2% compared to a state of the art method.
items.title: Decaf: A privacy preserving speech codec using speaker disentanglement and canonical voice conversion

items.summary: Speech remains intelligible to listeners under heavy temporal degradation, but whether speaker identity survives is largely unexplored. We evaluate six automatic speaker verification (ASV) models, trained on temporally intact speech, and tested under three degradations that remove different combinations of temporal cues. The models form three pairs, one per architecture family (convolutional, transformer, conformer), each pairing a waveform-input with a mel filterbank-input model. All models degrade, but robustness tracks input representation rather than pretraining scale or model size. In all nine family-by-condition comparisons the filterbank-input model degrades less, with eight of nine 95% confidence intervals excluding zero, even when it is smaller or has less pretraining than its waveform counterpart. In the controlled convolutional pair, where the models differ only in input representation, the filterbank-input model's equal error rate rises from 1.1% to 17.1% under the heaviest tested degradation, against 2.9% to29.7% for its waveform counterpart.
items.title: Input Representation, Not Model Size or Pretraining Scale, Shapes Speaker Verification Robustness to Temporal Degradation

items.summary: Speaker verification (SV) performance degrades under language mismatch due to the entanglement of speaker identity with language-specific acoustic cues. To address this problem, we leverage large-scale self-supervised pre-trained models (PTMs) to learn language-agnostic speaker representations. We utilize PTMs as robust front-end feature extractors, capitalizing on their rich acoustic and linguistic knowledge acquired from vast, diverse audio data. These generalized features are then used to train a downstream speaker embedding network, effectively disentangling speaker identity from language-specific characteristics. We validate our approach on the TidyVoice2026 benchmark, which benchmarks SV under language mismatch. Our proposed system (team T02) achieves equal error rates (EERs) of 2.21% on tv26_eval-A and 2.99% on tv26_eval-U.
items.title: Cross-Lingual Speaker Verification with Self-Supervised Pre-Trained Models

items.summary: We propose DeepASA, a multi-purpose model for auditory scene analysis that performs multi-input multi-output (MIMO) source separation, dereverberation, sound event detection (SED), audio classification, and direction-of-arrival estimation (DoAE) within a unified framework. DeepASA is designed for complex auditory scenes where multiple, often similar, sound sources overlap in time and move dynamically in space. To achieve robust and consistent inference across tasks, we introduce an object-oriented processing (OOP) strategy. This approach encapsulates diverse auditory features into object-centric representations and refines them through a chain-of-inference (CoI) mechanism. The pipeline comprises a dynamic temporal kernel-based feature extractor, a transformer-based aggregator, and an object separator that yields per-object features. These features feed into multiple task-specific decoders. Our object-centric representations naturally resolve the parameter association ambiguity inherent in traditional track-wise processing. However, early-stage object separation can lead to failure in downstream ASA tasks. To address this, we implement temporal coherence matching (TCM) within the chain-of-inference, enabling multi-task fusion and iterative refinement of object features using estimated auditory parameters. We evaluate DeepASA on representative spatial audio benchmark datasets, including ASA2, MC-FUSS, and STARSS23. Experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in both source separation and auditory parameter estimation under diverse spatial auditory scenes.
items.title: DeepASA: An Object-Oriented Multi-Purpose Network for Auditory Scene Analysis

items.summary: This repository provides the datasets, pretrained models and generated network parameters used in the manuscript “DiffPINN: Generative diffusion-initialized physics-informed neural networks for accelerating seismic wavefield representation.” The accompanying source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/DeepWave-KAUST/DiffPINN-pub DiffPINN is a latent diffusion framework that generates initialization parameters for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) used in frequency-domain seismic wavefield modeling. A set of PINNs is first trained across diverse velocity models and their parameters are flattened into one-dimensional vectors. An autoencoder compresses the length of these vectors into multi-channel latent tensors, and a conditional diffusion model is trained on those tensors with the velocity model and source configuration as conditions. At inference, the diffusion model generates a latent tensor for a new velocity model, with a physics-based gradient correction applied at each reverse step, and the decoder turns it into a complete set of PINN parameters. The archived files are organized as follows. dataset.zip After extraction, dataset.zip contains five folders corresponding to the five stages of the framework: metatrain/ : contains meta_train.mat , the dataset used for meta-training. pinntrain/ : contains pinntrain1.mat to pinntrain2600.mat , one file per velocity model, used to train the 2600 PINNs that form the parameter dataset. aetrain/ : contains the flattened parameters of the 2600 converged PINNs, used to train the autoencoder. difftrain/ : contains the latent tensors encoded from those parameters, used to train the diffusion model. pinntest/ : contains CurveVelA.mat , Layer.mat and FlatFaultA.mat , the three test velocity models used to reproduce the results reported in the manuscript. All data are stored in MATLAB .mat format. Each .mat file contains the following variables: x_train , z_train , sx_train : the spatial coordinates and source locations of the collocation samples. m_train , m0_train : the squared slowness of the medium and of the homogeneous background. u0_real_train , u0_imag_train : the real and imaginary parts of the analytical background wavefield. x_test , z_test , sx_test : the coordinates of the full evaluation grid. du_real_test , du_imag_test : the real and imaginary parts of the numerical reference solution. The training velocity models are drawn from the CurveVel-A class of the OpenFWI benchmark dataset, resized to 101×101 with a grid spacing of 25 m and mildly smoothed. All wavefields are computed at 5 Hz. The reference solutions are obtained with the optimized nine-point frequency-domain finite-difference scheme of Jo et al. (1996). Among the three test models, CurveVelA is drawn from the training distribution, while Layer (a layered section of the Marmousi model) and FlatFaultA lie outside it. Because aetrain/ and difftrain/ are the outputs of the two preceding stages, users can start at any point in the pipeline rather than rebuilding the parameter dataset, which takes roughly 65 hours on ten V100 GPUs. trained_model.zip After extraction, trained_model.zip contains the three trained models used to reproduce the results in the manuscript: meta_trained.pth : the meta-learned PINN initialization, trained for 40000 iterations over 500 velocity models. ae_trained.pth : the autoencoder, trained for 1000 epochs on the 2600 flattened parameter vectors. diff_trained.pt : the conditional diffusion model, trained for 400000 iterations on the latent tensors. generated_weight.zip After extraction, generated_weight.zip contains the latent tensors generated by the trained diffusion model for the three test velocity models: CurveVelA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the in-distribution CurveVel-A model. items.summary: LONGITUDINAL DEVICE MIGRATION AND MEANING CONTINUITY AT THE LIMIT Device Replacement × Model Bridging × Control Semantics STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 24 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli Research Works This research monograph investigates a deceptively difficult question in long-term brain–computer interfaces: when sensors, acquisition electronics, firmware, electrode geometry, or decoding models change, what would justify the claim that a user's task-grounded control meaning has been preserved? Numerical signal alignment alone cannot establish continuity of intention. Two systems may encode different signals while supporting the same functional command, or produce nearly identical latent representations while mapping to incompatible actions. The volume formulates meaning continuity as a conditional, falsifiable engineering and scientific hypothesis. It connects device-specific observation models, neural recording instability, task and action ontologies, paired old/new sensing periods, latent manifold bridging, longitudinal recalibration, calibrated abstention, functional validation, and an accessible right to reject the proposed migration. Its central commitment is that no amount of predictive accuracy can compensate for invalid authorization, an unverified physical reference, or loss of independent control. The research atlas comprises thirty connected mathematical derivations, eighty-two research chapters, and 410 independently paginated chapter sections that examine observables, inverse explanations, discriminating experiments, uncertainty and noncompensable safeguards, and independent requalification. Two hundred detailed Research Gates propose future falsification and handoff programs, while thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve revisable candidate approaches rather than immutable conclusions. A claim-scoped DOI evidence ledger connects the study to published work on neural recording drift, decoder adaptation, manifold alignment, longitudinal neural interfaces, speech BCIs, user preferences, and neurotechnology ethics. The book is designed for both human researchers and future AI research systems. Its formulas, chapter cross-links, DOI anchors, competing models, negative-result requirements, and successor-focused research cards provide structured entry points for independent reconstruction and informed disagreement. The visual presentation combines ivory pages, navy and teal typography, and large gold mathematical plates, while mathematical expressions are also recorded in searchable source notation and a separate Excel reference index. This is a prospective, nonclinical research architecture. It does not report new patient experiments, demonstrate safe autonomous human neurovascular microrobots, establish a universal device-migration system, or claim continuity of private thoughts, consciousness, or personal identity. Scientific benefit remains conditional on explicit task definitions, qualified device evidence, legitimate permissions, external validation, and the successor's freedom to reject a failed bridge. Research question: What should remain invariant when an interface changes, and who has the authority to say that its meaning has changed?

items.summary: Description This dataset accompanies a comparative evolutionary-genomics study of ancestral cytosine substitution patterns across human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla lineages. Using hg38-centered UCSC multiz primate alignments and a seven-species phylogenetic framework, we reconstructed ancestral nucleotide states and quantified cytosine substitutions across all 22 human autosomes. The analysis examined CG, CHG and CHH sequence contexts, 256 strand-canonicalized ancestral 5-mer motifs, and lineage-specific substitution patterns. The deposited files include: Chromosome-level ancestral-site datasets at a minimum ancestral-state posterior probability of 0.95. Chromosome-specific 5-mer substitution summaries and quality-control records. Genome-wide cytosine substitution frequencies and context-enrichment ratios. Chromosome-bootstrap uncertainty estimates and cross-lineage motif comparisons. Statistical analyses of lineage-specific motif deviations, including simultaneous confidence intervals. Leave-one-autosome-out predictive comparisons of ancestral 3-mer and 5-mer sequence context. Frozen methodology documentation, validation records, checksums and the fixed seven-species phylogenetic tree. The dataset supports independent examination and downstream reanalysis of the reported numerical findings. Data provenance: UCSC Genome Browser hg38-centered 30-primate multiz alignments, restricted to seven primate species. Computational methods: IQ-TREE 2.3.6 ancestral-state reconstruction under GTR+F+G4, followed by custom Python-based sequence-context and statistical analyses. Limitations: The archive contains processed ancestral-site data and numerical outputs, not the original complete multiple-sequence alignments. It does not contain ancestral DNA methylation measurements, direct estimates of net CpG gain or loss, or calibrated mutation rates. Associated code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23425960 Archive organization: This dataset is distributed across two Zenodo records. This record contains Part 1 of 2. Part 2 is available at https://zenodo.org/records/23442145 . Both parts are required to reconstruct the complete archive. Download all files from both records and follow the instructions in RECONSTRUCTION.txt to assemble and verify the dataset.
items.title: Ancestral Cytosine Sequence-Context Substitution Data Across Four Hominid Lineages: A 22-Autosome Comparative Analysis. Part 1

items.summary: This archive contains supplementary code, data, finite certificates, and reproduction instructions for “Merge Trees of Length-Filtered Lattice Knot Spaces” by Makoto Ozawa (arXiv:2605.25322). This release accompanies the 41-page revision prepared in October 2026 and preserves all files from the two supplementary archives published in the previous Zenodo version. The computations concern embedded polygons in the simple cubic lattice under standard BFACF moves. Polygons are identified under translations, proper cubic rotations, cyclic changes of starting point, and reversal of traversal; spatial reflections are retained. The archive includes the original implementations, seed files, search summaries, and explicit merge-path certificates, together with the complete minimal-layer material for the figure-eight knot and the knot 6_3. For the figure-eight knot, four minimal-layer components at length 30 merge into one component at cap 32. For 6_3, twelve minimal-layer components at length 40 merge into two mirror-related branches at cap 42 and one branch at cap 44. These statements concern the branches originating in the minimal layers, rather than an enumeration of every component at higher caps. The new trefoil supplement certifies six nonminimal components born at length 26 for a fixed chirality. Five first meet the minimal layer at cap 28, whereas a 20-state component first meets it at cap 30. The archive supplies closed component lists, capped-component separation certificates, explicit connecting paths, verification programs, and audit logs. The individual component and exact merge-height certificates do not assume exhaustion of the length-26 population; exhaustiveness at that level remains conditional on the reported literature population. The trefoil material also includes the actual BFACF path used in Figure 2: 47 configurations connected by 46 moves, with maximum length 30. All coordinates, the complete sequence of configurations, figure-generation code, and independent transition checks are provided. Additional checks verify coordinate spans of the specified trefoil components and singleton capped components for supplied 48-edge representatives of 8_3 and 8_7, including an improper spatial symmetry of the 8_3 representative. The release includes the corresponding manuscript source and figures, current documentation, checksums, provenance records, and a verification runner. Historical manuscripts are retained separately in the legacy directory; the current manuscript source is arxiv_revision/main.tex. items.summary: This paper offers a candidate descriptive model based on the author’s retrospective account of internal agent-like experience during a past period of social isolation, emotional distress and perceived high cognitive load. It is a non-clinical reconstruction, not a technique, treatment or recommendation. No contemporaneous physiological, behavioral or neuroimaging measurements were recorded. The Opposition–Load–Coupling vocabulary organizes reported phases of self-talk, opposition, felt load, perceived coupling, autonomy, boundary degradation and disengagement. These are reported experiences and interpretive constructs, not demonstrated causal mechanisms. Claimed benefits and harms are unmeasured first-person reports. The Shared Value Anchor is an untested candidate predictor, not an established stabilizer or necessary condition. The case does not establish whether value conflict preceded initial boundary degradation or distinguish the proposal from a simpler load-based account. The model is situated alongside dialogical-self, Internal Family Systems, predictive-processing, imaginary-companion, writer-agency and tulpa literature. Any incremental contribution lies in the proposed coupling vocabulary and separately testable value-anchor hypothesis, not in discovering internal multiplicity or proving a new mechanism. Safety: do not intentionally induce or replicate the conditions described. This is the author’s own past experience, published at the author’s direction; no formal ethics approval or exemption is claimed. Version 4 incorporates author-adopted revisions following advisory and changed-text checks, including prior-involved AI reviewers. Those checks are not independent peer review, clinical validation or evidence of effectiveness.

items.summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
items.title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

items.summary: mm-ADL-Home is a cross-environment millimeter-wave radar point-cloud dataset for human activity recognition in furnished residential environments. The dataset was collected in four indoor environments comprising three simulated bachelor-unit layouts and one real bachelor unit, using the same activity taxonomy and radar configuration as the mm-ADL dataset (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22405011).  Each participant–environment recording is preserved as a continuous point-cloud stream and includes: (1) point_cloud.csv , containing radar point-cloud observations; (2) frame_labels.csv , containing frame-level activity annotations; (3) timestamps.csv , providing the temporal correspondence between radar and annotation frames; and (4) location_annotations.csv , containing the intervals used to register the radar sensor and landmark furniture in the radar coordinate system. The activity taxonomy covers locomotion, sitting and lying transitions, stationary sitting and lying, simulated falls, and floor-to-standing recovery. Location annotations identify sittable furniture, lieable furniture, kitchen locations, entry locations, and the radar sensor origin. These annotations support the reconstruction of room-level spatial context and furniture landmarks on the horizontal radar coordinate plane. The dataset contains complete recordings without a prescribed windowing or segmentation scheme, allowing users to implement their own preprocessing, temporal segmentation, domain adaptation, and evaluation protocols. Synchronized RGB recordings used during annotation are not included in the public release. Participant identifiers are pseudonymous.
items.title: mm-ADL-Home: A Cross-Environment Millimeter-Wave Radar Point-Cloud Dataset for Activities of Daily Living in Furnished Homes

items.summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. items.summary: We develop a counterfactual semantics based on reopening partial information states. Evaluation first removes enough stated content to leave the antecedent’s attributes unresolved, retaining what the chosen scope protects, then asserts the antecedent and considers the surviving consistent refinements. Would and might quantify over the admissible alternatives; a weighted extension supplies graded evaluations. The principal result concerns finite models with fully supported residues. When a conjunctive antecedent reopens each constituent attribute, adding a supported conjunct can remove the grounds of another conclusion. A four-attribute countermodel therefore violates Cautious Monotony, excluding any smooth preferential representation that preserves the evaluable verdicts. We also establish a sufficient nesting condition for Cut and exhibit its failure without that condition. The conjunctive reopening rule is an explicit interpretive commitment; its suitability for ordinary-language counterfactuals remains an empirical question. The account uses declared dependencies, scope restrictions, and priorities, while the quantitative extension assumes a weight kernel. Comparisons with belief revision, premise semantics, update semantics, and causal intervention identify the consequences of reopening an attribute rather than merely making its proposed value consistent with retained information.
items.title: Counterfactual Evaluation by Reopening Information States

items.summary: Description This dataset accompanies a comparative evolutionary-genomics study of ancestral cytosine substitution patterns across human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla lineages. Using hg38-centered UCSC multiz primate alignments and a seven-species phylogenetic framework, we reconstructed ancestral nucleotide states and quantified cytosine substitutions across all 22 human autosomes. The analysis examined CG, CHG and CHH sequence contexts, 256 strand-canonicalized ancestral 5-mer motifs, and lineage-specific substitution patterns. The deposited files include: Chromosome-level ancestral-site datasets at a minimum ancestral-state posterior probability of 0.95. Chromosome-specific 5-mer substitution summaries and quality-control records. Genome-wide cytosine substitution frequencies and context-enrichment ratios. Chromosome-bootstrap uncertainty estimates and cross-lineage motif comparisons. Statistical analyses of lineage-specific motif deviations, including simultaneous confidence intervals. Leave-one-autosome-out predictive comparisons of ancestral 3-mer and 5-mer sequence context. Frozen methodology documentation, validation records, checksums and the fixed seven-species phylogenetic tree. The dataset supports independent examination and downstream reanalysis of the reported numerical findings. Data provenance: UCSC Genome Browser hg38-centered 30-primate multiz alignments, restricted to seven primate species. Computational methods: IQ-TREE 2.3.6 ancestral-state reconstruction under GTR+F+G4, followed by custom Python-based sequence-context and statistical analyses. Limitations: The archive contains processed ancestral-site data and numerical outputs, not the original complete multiple-sequence alignments. It does not contain ancestral DNA methylation measurements, direct estimates of net CpG gain or loss, or calibrated mutation rates. Associated code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23425960 Archive organization: This dataset is distributed across two Zenodo records. This record contains Part 1 of 2. Part 2 is available at https://zenodo.org/records/23442145 . Both parts are required to reconstruct the complete archive. items.summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.

items.summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. items.summary: Large language models often penalize multilingual users through hidden 'tokenizer taxes' caused by subword fragmentation. Geographic proper nouns offer a controlled stress case for this distributional asymmetry, as they are standardized, cross-linguistically available entities whose orthographic forms frequently mismatch tokenizer training distributions. We introduce the Cross-Linguistic Orthographic Uniqueness Score (CLOUS), a character-level metric based on Shannon surprisal that quantifies the orthographic rarity of localized country names. We evaluate CLOUS on a controlled corpus of 249 ISO-registered country names; generalization to other geographic entity types remains future work. We evaluate CLOUS against tokenization fertility for six production tokenizers spanning three algorithm families across eleven languages and seven script families. Using Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, CLOUS shows significant associative strength with fertility in 61 of 65 valid language-tokenizer combinations. As a screening tool for high-fragmentation entities, CLOUS achieves ROC-AUC = 0.850 and F1 = 0.740, correctly identifying approximately three-quarters of the highest-fragmentation entities from orthographic properties alone. We further show that CLOUS correlates with fertility more strongly than length-based baselines across all evaluated scripts, and outperforms a character bigram surprisal model in 69.2% of tested combinations, particularly for logographic, syllabic, and Latin scripts. Conversely, the bigram baseline proves superior for morphophonologically complex scripts like Arabic and Devanagari, indicating that tokenizer fragmentation is driven by local orthographic context in some scripts and absolute character rarity in others. Script family appears to be the primary driver of CLOUS-fertility correlation strength, with effect sizes ranging from modest for Latin-script languages ) to large for non-Latin scripts (   up to 0.686 for Japanese). These findings suggest that CLOUS may be useful as a lightweight pre-tokenization diagnostic for multilingual NLP pipelines.
items.title: Estimating Cross-Lingual Tokenization Fragmentation Risk: A Frequency-Based Uniqueness Score for Geographic Entities
